hero.title: The PN Diode
hero.lead: By joining a P-type semiconductor material to an N-type one, a PN junction is formed — the simplest semiconductor device, with the property of passing current in only one direction, the basis on which the junction diode is built.

objectives: Explains how the PN junction, the depletion region, and the potential barrier form.
Distinguishes between the forward-bias and reverse-bias states of the PN diode and the effect of each on current and resistance.
States the potential-barrier value for a diode made of silicon and of germanium, and names some types of diodes and their uses.

content.heading: 💡 5-3 The PN Diode
content.html:
Having seen in the previous section how an N-type semiconductor material works after antimony is added to it, and likewise how a P-type semiconductor material works after boron is added to it — and since a P-type and an N-type semiconductor material are each electrically neutral on their own, they do nothing by themselves.

A PN diode can therefore be obtained by doping a pure (silicon or germanium) crystal with two kinds of impurities: one trivalent (such as boron) and the other pentavalent (such as antimony). The dividing surface between the two regions is called the junction.

content.label: 📌 Definition — Depletion Region
content.html: Looking at Figure (5-9), we find that the electrons in the N region near the PN junction move toward the P region, leaving positive ions behind them; likewise, the holes in the P region near the PN junction move toward the N region, leaving negative ions behind them. As a result of this process, a thin region forms on both sides of the junction, containing positive ions in the N region and negative ions in the P region, called the depletion region.

content.heading: ⚡ Potential Barrier
content.html: As positive and negative ions continue to build up on both sides of the junction around this region (called the depletion or exhaustion layer), an electrically neutral equilibrium state is eventually reached. This produces an electric field whose resulting potential difference prevents additional electrons from crossing the PN junction, and so the diffusion of electrons stops; this barrier is called the potential barrier. An external voltage (a bias voltage) must therefore be applied to provide suitable conditions for the PN diode to operate.

content.heading: ↔️ Forward Bias and Reverse Bias
content.html:
When the P region is connected to the positive terminal of the battery and the N region to the negative terminal, the PN diode is said to be forward-biased — that is, a large current flows through the PN junction, called the forward current, because the resistance of the PN diode is small.

When, instead, the P region is connected to the negative terminal of the battery and the N region to the positive terminal, the PN diode is said to be reverse-biased — that is, a very small current flows through the PN junction, called the reverse current (which can be neglected), because the resistance of the PN diode is large.

content.heading: 🔌 The Junction Diode
content.html:
The junction diode is one of the simplest semiconductor devices, and it has the property of passing current in only one direction. The effect described above occurs even without an external voltage across the actual junction, and the result is that the junction reaches a state of equilibrium. However, if the terminals of the negative and positive materials are connected to an external source, an additional energy source becomes available to overcome the barrier, enabling free electrons to cross the depletion region from one side to the other.

The depletion layer widens as the applied reverse voltage increases, owing to the difference in electrical properties on the two sides of the junction; this results in the rectification of alternating current — for example, into a single unidirectional rectified current.

content.html: The potential barrier of a PN diode at room temperature (300 K) equals (0.7 V) for one made of silicon, and (0.3 V) for one made of germanium. There are several types of diodes, including: a- the light-sensitive diode. b- the photovoltaic (photocell) diode. c- the light-emitting diode. d- the current-rectifying diode.

content.descriptionHtml: Choose a bias state and observe the width of the depletion region and the direction and magnitude of the current flowing through the PN junction.

ruleBoxes.html: Forward bias (P on positive, N on negative): the depletion region narrows and the resistance drops, so a large forward current flows.

labels.captionNone: With no external bias: the depletion region settles at a fixed width, and no net current flows across the junction.
labels.captionForward: Forward bias (P on positive, N on negative): the depletion region narrows and the resistance drops, so a large forward current flows.
labels.captionReverse: Reverse bias (P on negative, N on positive): the depletion region widens and the resistance rises, so only a tiny, negligible reverse current flows.

questions.question: The depletion region arises as a result of:
options: Electrons moving from N to P and holes moving from P to N around the junction
Shining an external light on the diode
An increase in the number of silicon atoms
questions.explain: Electrons in the N region near the junction move to the P region, leaving positive ions, and holes in the P region move to the N region, leaving negative ions — forming the depletion region.

questions.question: When the P region is connected to the battery's positive terminal and the N region to the negative terminal, the diode is:
questions.explain: Connecting P to positive and N to negative gives forward bias, so the diode's resistance becomes small and a large forward current flows.

questions.question: The potential barrier for a diode made of silicon at room temperature (300 K) equals:
questions.explain: The potential barrier equals (0.7 V) for a diode made of silicon, and (0.3 V) for one made of germanium, at (300 K).

questions.question: The essential property of the junction diode is:
options: Passing current equally in both directions
Passing current in only one direction
questions.explain: The junction diode is one of the simplest semiconductor devices, and it has the property of passing current in only one direction.

summary.heading: 📋 Lesson Summary
items: The PN diode forms by doping a pure crystal with two impurities (trivalent and pentavalent) on two neighboring regions, separated by the junction.
Depletion region: a thin layer around the junction containing positive ions in N and negative ions in P, giving rise to the potential barrier that prevents further electron diffusion.
Forward bias (P on positive, N on negative): small resistance and a large forward current. Reverse bias: large resistance and a very small, negligible reverse current.
Potential barrier at 300K: (0.7 V) for silicon and (0.3 V) for germanium.
The junction diode (diode) passes current in only one direction; its types include the light-sensitive diode, the photocell diode, the light-emitting diode, and the current-rectifying diode.
